headline: Holgate's inside cut is choking on peanut bunker — blues and weaks are stacked on the flood
subhead: The bunker finally pushed south into the bay like we said it would, and now every cut from Beach Haven to Graveling Point has bait pinned against the marsh.
body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate cut Tuesday morning at low and the bottom told me everything I needed to know before I even wet a line. The inside bar that's been building all summer has finally pinched down into a real trough — maybe four feet deep at dead low, tight against the beach, and it was black with peanut bunker getting pushed up against the sand by something bigger working the deep side. That's the signature I look for this time of year. The outer bar's still soft and shifting from all the southerly wind swell we've had — buoy readings off the coast have been running 3 to 4 feet at short six-second intervals, which is just wind chop stacking on itself, not a real groundswell. It's kept the ocean side mediocre for plugging, but it's pushed all that bait tight to structure, and the back bay and inlet cuts are where the money's been.

We flagged this a few days back — said the bunker schools drifting down from the Manasquan corridor would spill into LBI's bays and light up the blues, and that's exactly what's happening. Snapper blues are thick from the Ship Bottom bulkheads down through Beach Haven, chopping bait on the surface most evenings on the last two hours of the outgoing. But it's not just snappers anymore — I'm seeing cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound class mixed in at Holgate and around the Causeway bridge pilings, hitting small metal-lipped swimmers and 1/4-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the peanut schools. If you want a family afternoon, that's your ticket — light spinning gear, no wire needed for the snappers, small hooks on bait or tiny poppers.

Weakfish are doing what weakfish do in August — they've slid in behind that same peanut bunker push, and the reports out of the deeper holes in Great Bay and along the Mullica channel edges have been better than I expected for this time of year. Nothing giant, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but they're eating. Best bite has been the last of the incoming into the top of the tide, drifting small Bass Assassins in pearl or bunker colors on 1/4-ounce jigheads through 8 to 12 feet of water off Graveling Point and the mouth of the Mullica. Slow retrieve, let it sink, twitch it back — weaks want it subtle, not ripped.

Fluke are still the most consistent bottom bite in the zone, but they've abandoned the shallow flats entirely with this heat. Barnegat Inlet's north and south edges are holding fish in 15 to 25 feet on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current really rips and stacks bait against the rocks. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, tipped with a fresh spearing strip if you've got it — that combo's been putting keepers in the box, mostly 17 to 20 inches with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in. Little Egg Inlet's channel edges are fishing the same way on the outgoing, especially the drop-off just inside the rocks where the sand gives way to that harder bottom.

Striper fishing has settled into the summer pattern we all know and don't love — it's a night game now. Surface water's sitting warm enough that the bass have gone deep and nocturnal, holding around the bridge structure at the Causeway and the deeper holes off Beach Haven, feeding hard on bunker after dark. If you're serious about a keeper bass right now, that means bunker chunks or live bunker under the lights on the bridge, fished on the bottom during the tide change, or working a swimming plug slow through the pilings at 10 or 11 at night when the current's moving. Daytime bass are mostly a wishful-thinking proposition through the heat.

Kingfish are still showing on the ocean side sandbars, particularly the troughs off Ship Bottom and Surf City where that inside cut structure I mentioned holds up. Bloodworm and Fishbites on a high-low rig, cast into the trough on the incoming, has been steady if unspectacular — good action for kids and a nice change of pace between fluke drifts.

As for the bonito watch — the ocean's sitting right at 75.9 degrees off the coast, which is exactly the number that usually tips the first false albacore or bonito sightings on LBI's outer bars. Nothing confirmed yet, but with that kind of surface temp and bait already staging in the cuts, I wouldn't be shocked to hear reports out of the Barnegat Light rips within the next week or two. Worth keeping a small metal in the plug bag just in case.

Looking ahead, if this southerly wind pattern holds and keeps stacking short-period swell on the outer bar, I'd keep my effort inside — the inlets and back bay cuts are where the bait is and where the fish are eating. If the wind backs off and the ocean lays down flat for a stretch, that's when I'd run the beach at first light looking for albie signs on the bar breaks. Either way, watch that tide — everything worth catching this week wants moving water.
